newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Supreme Court hears school religion arguments.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Supreme Court hears school religion arguments.

text.p: The Supreme Court considered an important church-state case on Tuesday, grappling with how far to go in allowing government aid to religious school students across the country.

The justices pressed lawyers on both sides of the dispute on where exactly they should draw the line in the contentious issue of what type of public aid may be provided to students at private religious schools.

Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger, the Clinton administration's top courtroom lawyer, urged the justices to overturn a 12-year-old ruling that bars public school teachers from conducting remedial classes at parochial schools.
But Justice David Souter questioned whether public school teachers then could be sent into parochial schools to teach reading or mathematics. "How do we draw the line?" he asked repeatedly.

Dellinger said the program involved federal money designed to be a supplement to benefit low-income, needy children, and that it did not rise to the level of taking over a private school's curriculum.
But when Souter pressed further on whether the government thought it appropriate to provide money for the teaching of a secular subject at a parochial school, Dellinger replied, "We do not."

At issue during the hour-long arguments was a 1985 Supreme Court ruling that publicly paid teachers may not offer remedial classes on parochial school grounds because it violates the constitutional requirement on church-state separation.

But the court has become more conservative over the past 12 years, lowering the wall of separation between church and state. A majority of the court's current nine members have advocated overturning the 1985 decision.
Paul Crotty, a New York City lawyer who also argued against the 1985 ruling, said 260,000 children in the city receive help under the remedial program.
Of the total, about 22,000 attend parochial schools, but they must be taught in buses or by computers because of the 1985 ruling, he said.

If public school teachers were allowed into parochial schools, Justice Stephen Breyer asked him, "Where exactly is the line" on what they can teach? Crotty answered that it would be only remedial courses authorized under the program.
Stanley Geller, an attorney for the six individuals who won the 1985 ruling, said the current case, because of procedural problems, cannot be used by the Supreme Court to overrule its 1985 decision.
Justice Antonin Scalia asked why public school teachers should be allowed in buses, but not in parochial school classrooms. "What happens from the bus to the classroom?"
Geller replied that he opposes allowing the teachers even on buses, but added that his challenge to that was pending before a U.S. appeals court in New York. "That's another case," he said.
After the arguments, the justices took the matter under advisement, with a ruling due by the end of their term in June.
